name: Asynchronous JavaScript
author: Recurse
subject: programming
description: The event loop, callbacks and timers, promises and Promise.all, async/await, fetch and JSON, and the common async bugs.

lesson.intro: Network requests, timers, file reads and user clicks all finish at unpredictable times, and JavaScript handles them without ever blocking its single thread. This lesson explains how: the event loop with its task and microtask queues, callbacks and timers, promises and their combinators, async/await, fetching JSON from an API, and the async bugs that show up again and again in code reviews and interviews.
objectives: Explain the event loop and predict the output order of synchronous code, timers and promise callbacks
Chain promises with then, catch and finally, and wrap callback APIs in promises
Run work in parallel with Promise.all, and choose allSettled, race or any when they fit better
Write async functions with await and try/catch, and fetch JSON while checking the response status
Recognize and fix common async bugs: missing await, needless sequential awaits, async forEach and unhandled rejections

sections.title: Why JavaScript is asynchronous
sections.body:
Click a button that loads your profile, and the page stays responsive while the data travels across the network for half a second. That only works because JavaScript doesn't wait for the network, and understanding how it avoids waiting is the key to everything in this lesson.

JavaScript runs your code on a **single thread**: one call stack, one thing at a time. In a browser, that same thread also handles clicks, scrolling and redrawing the page. If your code stopped and waited 500 ms for a response, nothing else could happen for those 500 ms: no clicks, no animation, a frozen tab. Code that holds the thread while it waits is called **blocking**.

So JavaScript hands slow work to its host environment. The browser (or Node.js) runs timers, network requests and file reads outside your code. Your code registers what should happen when the result is ready, a **callback**, and carries straight on. When the work finishes, the environment queues your callback, and the **event loop** runs it once the thread is free.

That gives JavaScript its characteristic execution order: everything synchronous in the current code runs to completion first, and callbacks run later, even a timer set to 0 ms. The code is **non-blocking**: starting an operation and receiving its result happen at different times.

Three generations of tools manage that gap, and you'll meet all three in real code:
- **Callbacks**: pass a function to be called later. Simple, but deeply nested steps get messy.
- **Promises**: objects representing a future value, which you can chain and combine.
- **async/await**: syntax on top of promises that lets asynchronous code read top to bottom like ordinary code.

Asynchronous is not the same as parallel. Your JavaScript never runs two callbacks at the same instant; it interleaves them. That's why a long synchronous loop, such as sorting a million items, still freezes the page: the event loop can't run anything else until it finishes. Heavy computation belongs in a Web Worker in the browser, or a worker thread in Node.
sections.pitfall: Thinking async code runs in parallel with your other JavaScript. Callbacks take turns on one thread, so a long synchronous loop still freezes everything.

check.question: JavaScript runs on a single thread. How does a page stay responsive while a network request is in flight?
choices: JavaScript starts a new thread for every request
The request blocks only part of the page
The environment performs the request outside your code and queues a callback for when it finishes
The CPU pauses the request whenever the user clicks
check.explanation: The browser or Node does the waiting. Your code only runs again, through the event loop, when the result is ready, so the thread stays free for clicks and rendering in the meantime.

sections.title: The event loop: tasks and microtasks
sections.body:
Quick: what does this print? `console.log("A"); setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("C")); console.log("D");` The answer is A, D, C, B, and the reason is the event loop's two queues. Interviewers love this question because it tests whether you really understand how JavaScript schedules work.

The pieces:
- The **call stack** holds the functions currently running. Your script's top-level code is the first entry.
- The **task queue** (also called the macrotask or callback queue) holds callbacks from timers, I/O and UI events such as clicks.
- The **microtask queue** holds promise callbacks (`then`, `catch`, `finally`, and the code after an `await`) plus anything passed to `queueMicrotask`.

The loop follows one rule, over and over:
- Run the current task (at first, your whole script) until the call stack is empty.
- Run **every** microtask, including microtasks queued by other microtasks, until the queue is empty.
- In a browser, update the screen if needed.
- Take the **next** task from the task queue and repeat.

So synchronous code always finishes first. Then promise callbacks, all of them. Then timers, one at a time, each followed by its own microtasks. `setTimeout(fn, 0)` means "queue fn as a task as soon as possible", which is always after the current code and after every pending microtask.

Two consequences matter in practice. A timer's delay is a minimum, not a guarantee: if the thread is busy, the callback waits, and browsers also stretch deeply nested short timers to about 4 ms. And because microtasks run before the next task, a promise chain that keeps queuing microtasks can starve timers and rendering. It's rare, but it explains some frozen pages.

To trace an ordering question by hand, keep three columns: the call stack, the microtask queue and the task queue. Process the script, drain the microtasks, take one task, drain again. With a little practice it becomes quick.
sections.pitfall: Assuming `setTimeout(fn, 0)` runs right away. It always waits for the current code and every pending promise callback.

activity.title: Fix the order with one change
activity.prompt: Predict the current output before you run it, using the three-column method. Then change exactly one line so the numbers come out 1 to 5. Hint: which number would have to stop being a timer callback?

props.task: Change one line so the program logs 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 in order.

check.question: After the current script finishes, which runs first: a setTimeout(fn, 0) callback or a Promise.resolve().then(fn) callback?
choices: The timer, because it was scheduled with 0 ms
The promise callback, because all microtasks run before the next task
Whichever appears first in the code
They run at the same time
check.explanation: Promise callbacks are microtasks, and the event loop drains the whole microtask queue before taking the next task, such as a timer callback. Source order only matters within the same queue.

sections.title: Callbacks and timers
sections.body:
Before promises, asynchronous JavaScript was written entirely with **callbacks**: functions you pass to an API so it can call them when something happens. They're still everywhere: event listeners, array methods, timers and many Node.js APIs.

Timers are the simplest example:
- `setTimeout(fn, ms)` calls fn once, after at least ms milliseconds, and returns an id.
- `setInterval(fn, ms)` calls fn repeatedly, roughly every ms milliseconds, until stopped.
- `clearTimeout(id)` and `clearInterval(id)` cancel them. An interval you never clear runs forever, which in a long-lived page or component is a classic memory leak.

Extra arguments after the delay are passed to the callback. The callback also sees whatever variables it closed over, which is why the var-in-a-loop closure bug from JavaScript Basics bites hardest with timers.

Node.js popularized the **error-first callback** convention: the callback's first parameter is an error (or null), and the result comes second, as in `fs.readFile(path, "utf8", (err, data) => { ... })`. Always check err first; ignoring it is the callback version of an unhandled exception.

Callbacks get painful when steps depend on each other. Load a user, then their orders, then the first order's items: each step nests inside the previous one's callback, and the code drifts right in a pyramid known as **callback hell**. Error handling has to be repeated at every level. There's also a subtler problem called **inversion of control**: you hand your continuation to someone else's code and trust it to call it exactly once, never twice and never zero times.

Promises were designed to fix exactly these problems: flat chains instead of nesting, one place to handle errors, and a guarantee that a result is delivered at most once. You'll still write callbacks daily (every event handler is one), but for "do this, then that" sequences, reach for promises and async/await.
sections.pitfall: Starting a setInterval without keeping its id. You can never stop it, and it keeps running, and holding memory, after you no longer need it.

activity.title: Stop the countdown
activity.prompt: Run it: the interval never stops, so the playground cuts it off after a few seconds. Keep the id that setInterval returns, and when n reaches 0, clear the interval and log liftoff.

props.task: Make the program log 3, 2, 1 and then liftoff, and stop.

check.question: In Node's error-first callback convention, what is the first argument passed to the callback?
choices: The number of retries so far
An error, or null if the operation succeeded
check.explanation: Putting the error first forces you to look at it: if (err) handle it, otherwise use the result in the second argument.

sections.title: Promises: then, catch and chaining
sections.body:
A **promise** is an object that stands for a value you'll have later: a server's response, the contents of a file. Instead of passing a callback into the operation, the operation returns a promise, and you attach what should happen next.

A promise is always in one of three states:
- **pending**: the operation hasn't finished.
- **fulfilled**: it succeeded, with a value.
- **rejected**: it failed, with a reason, usually an Error.

Once fulfilled or rejected, it's **settled** and never changes again. That fixes a callback weakness: a result is delivered exactly once.

`promise.then(onFulfilled)` registers a callback for the value, `.catch(onRejected)` for the error, and `.finally(fn)` for cleanup either way. These callbacks always run asynchronously, as microtasks, even when the promise has already settled.

The key fact is that **`then` returns a new promise**, and that's what makes chaining work:
- If your callback returns a plain value, the next `then` receives it.
- If it returns a promise, the chain waits for that promise and passes on its result. This is how you sequence async steps without nesting.
- If it throws, or returns a rejected promise, the chain skips ahead to the next `catch`.

So one `catch` at the end handles a failure from any earlier step, just as one try/catch can surround several lines. After a catch handles an error, the chain continues as fulfilled with whatever the catch returned.

You create promises with `new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... })`, calling resolve(value) on success or reject(error) on failure. You'll mainly do this to wrap old callback APIs, like turning setTimeout into a `wait(ms)` function. `Promise.resolve(v)` and `Promise.reject(err)` make already-settled promises.

The most common chaining bug is forgetting to `return` inside a `then`. The inner operation starts, but the chain doesn't wait for it, and the next step receives undefined.
sections.pitfall: Forgetting to return a promise from inside then. The chain stops waiting for it, and the next step receives undefined.

activity.title: Repair a broken chain
activity.prompt: Run it and look at the result: the second step starts a promise but doesn't return it, so the chain moves on with undefined. Add the missing return and run again.

props.task: Make the program log exactly: result: 20

check.question: What does .then(callback) return?
choices: A new promise that settles with the callback's result
The value passed to its callback
The same promise it was called on
check.explanation: Every then creates a new promise. It fulfills with the callback's return value (waiting for it if that value is itself a promise), or rejects if the callback throws, which is what lets steps chain.

sections.title: Combining promises: all, allSettled, race and any
sections.body:
A dashboard needs the user, their notifications and today's stats. The three requests don't depend on each other, so waiting for each one before starting the next wastes time: three 200 ms requests in sequence take 600 ms, while in parallel they take about 200 ms. Promise combinators let you start several operations at once and decide how to wait for them.

Each takes an array (any iterable) of promises and returns one promise:
- `Promise.all(promises)` fulfills with an array of all the values, **in the same order as the input**, whichever finished first. If any one rejects, it rejects immediately with that error, which is called failing fast. The other operations keep running, but their results are ignored.
- `Promise.allSettled(promises)` waits for every promise and never rejects. Each result is an object, `{ status: "fulfilled", value }` or `{ status: "rejected", reason }`. Use it when partial success is useful, such as showing whichever widgets loaded.
- `Promise.race(promises)` settles like the first promise to settle, whether it fulfills or rejects. The classic use is a timeout: race the request against a promise that rejects after 5 seconds.
- `Promise.any(promises)` fulfills with the first promise to fulfill, and rejects (with an AggregateError) only if they all reject. Use it for "whichever mirror answers first".

The operations are already running by the time you pass their promises in: calling `fetch` starts the request, and the combinator only decides how you wait. That's why `Promise.all(ids.map(id => getUser(id)))` is the standard parallel pattern, because map starts every request immediately.

Parallel isn't always right. If step two needs step one's result, it has to wait. And firing 10,000 requests at once can overwhelm a server or hit rate limits, so real code often processes big lists in batches, say ten at a time.
sections.code:
const wait = (ms, value) => new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r(value), ms));
const fail = (ms, msg) => new Promise((_, reject) => setTimeout(() => reject(new Error(msg)), ms));

Promise.all([wait(30, "user"), wait(10, "stats")])
  .then(values => console.log("all:", values));            // all: ["user", "stats"]

Promise.all([wait(30, "user"), fail(10, "stats down")])
  .catch(err => console.log("all failed:", err.message));   // all failed: stats down

Promise.allSettled([wait(20, "user"), fail(5, "stats down")])
  .then(results => console.log(results.map(r => r.status))); // ["fulfilled", "rejected"]

Promise.race([wait(50, "slow"), wait(15, "fast")])
  .then(v => console.log("race:", v));                     // race: fast

// Logged in order of completion: all failed, race, allSettled, all
sections.pitfall: Using Promise.all when one failure shouldn't sink the rest. It rejects on the first error; use allSettled for best-effort work.

check.question: Promise.all receives three promises, and the second one rejects before the others finish. What happens?
choices: It waits for all three, then rejects
It fulfills with the two successful values
It rejects right away with the second promise's error
check.explanation: Promise.all fails fast: the first rejection rejects the combined promise. The other operations still run, but their results are discarded. allSettled is the combinator that waits for everything.

sections.title: async and await
sections.body:
Promise chains are a big improvement on callbacks, but they still read differently from ordinary code. **async/await** lets you write asynchronous steps top to bottom, with normal variables, loops and try/catch.

Mark a function `async` and two things change:
- It **always returns a promise**. `return 5` inside it fulfills that promise with 5, and a `throw` rejects it.
- You can use `await` inside it. `await somePromise` pauses this function until the promise settles, then gives you the fulfilled value, or throws the rejection reason on that line, exactly as if the line had thrown.

Pausing is the crucial idea: `await` suspends only the async function it's in. The thread is released, the event loop keeps running other code, and when the promise settles, the rest of the function continues as a microtask. Nothing blocks.

Errors use plain `try/catch/finally` around the awaited lines, which is often the biggest readability win over `.catch()`. Code after an `await` inside `try` only runs if the awaited promise fulfilled.

Because an async function returns a promise, its caller must `await` it (or use `.then`) to get the result, which is why async tends to spread up through a codebase. At the very top, ES modules and modern Node allow **top-level await**; older scripts call an async `main()` function instead. The playground in this app runs classic scripts, so its examples use the `main()` style.

Sequencing comes naturally: two awaits in a row run one after the other. To run independent operations in parallel, start them first and await them together: `const [user, posts] = await Promise.all([getUser(id), getPosts(id)]);`.

Awaiting something that isn't a promise just gives the value back after a microtask, so `await` on a function that forgot to return its promise silently waits for nothing.
sections.pitfall: Calling an async function without await and using the result as if it were the value. You get a Promise object, not the data.

check.question: An async function's body runs return 42. What does calling the function give you?
check.explanation: async functions always return a promise. The return value becomes the fulfilled value, so the caller writes await f() or f().then(...) to get 42.

sections.title: fetch and JSON
sections.body:
Most asynchronous code in web apps talks to an HTTP API, and in browsers and modern Node that means `fetch`. It's promise based, and it has two quirks that catch almost everyone.

`fetch(url)` starts a request and returns a promise for a **Response**. The Response arrives as soon as the status and headers do; the body may still be downloading. Reading the body is a second asynchronous step: `await res.json()` parses it as JSON, and `await res.text()` returns it as text.

**Quirk one: fetch doesn't reject on HTTP errors.** A 404 or a 500 is a successful exchange of messages as far as fetch is concerned, so its promise fulfills. It rejects only on network failure: no connection, a DNS error, a CORS block or an aborted request. Check `res.ok` (true for statuses 200 to 299) or `res.status` yourself, and throw when it isn't what you expect.

**Quirk two: the body is a promise too.** `res.json()` returns a promise, so you need a second `await`. Forgetting it gives you a pending Promise where you expected data.

To send data, pass an options object with the method, headers and body. A JavaScript object must be turned into a string with `JSON.stringify`, and the `Content-Type: application/json` header tells the server what you're sending.

fetch has no built-in timeout. An `AbortController` cancels a request: pass its `signal` to fetch and call `controller.abort()` after a deadline, or pass `AbortSignal.timeout(5000)` in modern runtimes. Aborting makes fetch reject, which your catch can handle.

A pattern worth memorizing is a small helper that does all of this once (fetch, check `ok`, parse JSON, throw a useful error) so the rest of your code can simply `await getJSON(url)`. In the browser you'll also meet **CORS**: a page may only read a response from another origin if that server allows it with the right headers. That's a server setting, not something your fetch call can override.
sections.pitfall: Assuming fetch rejects on a 404 or 500. It doesn't; check `res.ok` and throw yourself.

activity.title: Handle a 404 like fetch returns it
activity.prompt: The playground blocks real network requests, so fakeFetch imitates fetch, including fulfilling for a 404. In loadUser, throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`) when res.ok is false. Then add a catch to the second call that logs failed: and the message.

props.task: Make the program log Ada and then failed: HTTP 404.

check.question: Why does reading the body need a second await, as in const data = await res.json()?
choices: res.json() returns a promise, because the body may still be downloading and must be parsed
Because fetch always returns its data twice
Because JSON must be validated by the server first
It doesn't; res.json() returns the data directly
check.explanation: The Response arrives once the headers do, before the whole body has. res.json() reads and parses the body asynchronously, so it returns a promise you have to await.

sections.title: Common async bugs
sections.body:
Most async bugs fall into a handful of patterns. Learn to recognize them and you'll fix them in minutes instead of hours, and spot them in code review before they ship.

**Forgetting await.** `const user = getUser(1);` gives you a Promise, not a user, so `user.name` is undefined, and logging it shows a pending promise. Worse, an async call made without awaiting, such as `saveDraft()`, can fail with nobody listening. Linters catch this (typescript-eslint's no-floating-promises rule, for example).

**Sequential awaits that should be parallel.** `const a = await getA(); const b = await getB();` waits for A before even starting B. If they're independent, start both and await them together with `Promise.all`. On the other hand, awaiting inside a `for...of` loop is correct when each step needs the previous one, or when you deliberately want one request at a time.

**async callbacks in forEach.** `items.forEach(async item => { await save(item); })` does not wait: forEach ignores the promises its callback returns, so the code after it runs immediately, and errors go unhandled. Use `for...of` with await for sequential work, or `await Promise.all(items.map(...))` for parallel work.

**Unhandled rejections.** A rejected promise that nothing handles becomes an unhandled rejection. Browsers log it, and Node.js (since version 15) crashes the process by default. Every chain needs a catch at the end, and every awaited call needs a try/catch somewhere above it.

**Mixing styles.** Combining `.then` callbacks and `await` in one function works, but it's easy to lose a return or a catch. Pick one style per function; await is usually clearer.

**Stale responses.** A user types "ca" and then "cat", and the slower "ca" response arrives last and overwrites the results. Track the latest request (with a counter or an AbortController) and ignore or cancel older ones. This race condition is a favorite topic in front-end interviews.
sections.pitfall: Using forEach with an async callback and expecting it to wait. It returns immediately; use for...of, or Promise.all with map.

activity.title: Fix an async forEach
activity.prompt: Run it: results is still empty when it's logged, because forEach doesn't wait for async callbacks. Replace the forEach with await Promise.all(ids.map(...)), which runs the requests in parallel and keeps the results in input order.

props.task: Make the program log exactly: results: [300, 100, 200]

check.question: items.forEach(async item => { await save(item); }); console.log("saved"); When does saved print?
check.explanation: forEach calls each async callback, gets back a promise, and ignores it. The loop ends at once, so saved prints while the saves are still in flight.

keyTerms.definition: Starting slow work without waiting for it, so the single thread stays free.
A function passed to an API so it can be called later, when something happens.
The mechanism that runs queued callbacks whenever the call stack is empty.
Where timer, I/O and UI event callbacks wait; one task runs per loop turn.
A promise callback or code after await; all queued microtasks run before the next task.
An object for a future value: pending, then fulfilled with a value or rejected with a reason.
A promise that has fulfilled or rejected; its state never changes again.
Waits for every promise and gives their values in input order; rejects on the first failure.
Waits for every promise and reports each outcome; it never rejects.
A function that always returns a promise and may use await inside.
Pauses the current async function until a promise settles, then gives its value or throws.
A rejected promise with no handler; logged by browsers and fatal in Node by default.

summary: JavaScript runs on one thread: slow work happens in the environment, and callbacks run later through the event loop.
After the current code, every microtask (promise callback) runs before the next task (timers, events).
then returns a new promise: return values or promises to chain steps, and one catch at the end handles any failure.
Promise.all runs work in parallel and fails fast; allSettled, race and any cover partial success, timeouts and first wins.
async functions always return promises; await pauses only that function, and try/catch handles rejections.
fetch fulfills even for 404 and 500 and needs a second await for the body; watch for missing awaits, async forEach and unhandled rejections.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who knows basic JavaScript why console.log("A"); setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("C")); console.log("D"); prints A D C B, and what await actually pauses.

questions.question: What does this log, in order? Write the three numbers separated by spaces.
questions.explanation: The timer callback is queued as a task, and tasks only run after the current code finishes, so 3 prints before 2 even with a 0 ms delay.

questions.question: A page uses fetch and promises everywhere, yet clicking a Sort button freezes it for two seconds. What is the most likely cause?
choices: fetch requests block the thread while they run
Promises always pause the page while they are pending
The sort is a long synchronous computation, and the event loop can't run anything else until it finishes
The browser limits pages to one event listener at a time
questions.explanation: Async APIs keep waiting off the thread, but your own JavaScript still runs on it. A long synchronous loop holds the call stack, so clicks and rendering wait. Move heavy work to a Web Worker or split it into chunks.

questions.question: Which of these are handled by the environment outside your JavaScript, with a callback queued when they finish? Select all that apply.
choices: A for loop over an array
questions.explanation: Timers, network I/O and UI events are tracked by the browser or Node, which queues your callbacks when they happen. Loops and sort are ordinary synchronous JavaScript that runs on the thread until done.

questions.question: In what order are the letters logged? Write them separated by spaces.
questions.explanation: A and D are synchronous. The promise callback C is a microtask, which runs as soon as the script finishes. The timer B is a task, which waits until the microtask queue is empty.

questions.question: In what order are these logged?
questions.explanation: Each task is followed by a full drain of the microtask queue. The first timer logs t1 and queues p1, which runs before the event loop takes the second timer, so t2 comes last.

questions.question: In what order are these logged?
choices: before, f start, f end, after
before, after, f start, f end
before, f start, after, f end
f start, before, after, f end
questions.explanation: An async function runs synchronously until its first await, so f start prints right away. The await pauses f and returns control, so after prints, and the rest of f runs later as a microtask.

questions.question: Put one turn of the event loop in order.
items: Run the current task, such as the script, until the call stack is empty
Run every queued microtask until that queue is empty
Update the screen if needed (in a browser)
Take the next task from the task queue
questions.explanation: This cycle explains every ordering puzzle: synchronous code first, then all promise callbacks, then rendering, then exactly one timer or event callback, and repeat.

questions.question: What does this log?
questions.explanation: clearTimeout cancels the first timer before it fires, so only B is logged. A cancelled timer's callback never runs.

questions.question: This should log tick three times and stop, but it never stops. Why?
choices: count === 3 is never true because count is reset each time
setInterval only stops when the page reloads
The delay must be at least 1000 ms
clearInterval needs the id that setInterval returned: const id = setInterval(...), then clearInterval(id)
questions.explanation: Called with no id, clearInterval has nothing to cancel and quietly does nothing. Keep the returned id and pass it in. count does reach 3; the interval just ignores the empty clear.

questions.question: In this Node.js callback, what should the code do first?
choices: Check err, and handle it before touching data
Call readFile again to confirm the result
questions.explanation: In the error-first convention, err is null on success and an Error on failure, in which case data is undefined. Parsing first would crash on a missing file. Returning from a callback doesn't reach the original caller anyway.

questions.question: What is callback hell, and how do promises improve on it?
questions.answer: Callback hell is deeply nested callbacks for dependent async steps, with error handling repeated at every level. Promises flatten the steps into a chain, handle errors in one catch, and guarantee each result is delivered exactly once.
questions.explanation: async/await goes one step further, letting the same sequence read like ordinary top-to-bottom code with try/catch.

questions.question: A promise has fulfilled with the value 5. Can it later become rejected?
choices: Yes, if the code calls reject afterwards
No: once a promise settles, its state and value never change
Yes, if a then callback throws
Only if it was created with new Promise
questions.explanation: Settling is permanent, and later calls to resolve or reject are ignored. A throwing then callback rejects the new promise that then returned, not the original one.

questions.question: What does this log?
questions.code:
Promise.resolve(2)
  .then(n => n * 3)
  .then(n => { n + 1; })
  .then(n => console.log(n));
questions.explanation: The second callback uses braces without return, so it returns undefined, and that's what the next then receives. Writing n => n + 1 would pass 7.

questions.question: What does this log?
questions.code:
Promise.reject(new Error("x"))
  .then(() => console.log("A"))
  .catch(() => "B")
  .then(v => console.log(v))
  .finally(() => console.log("C"));
questions.explanation: The rejection skips the first then. catch handles it and returns "B", so the chain continues as fulfilled with "B", which the next then logs. finally runs at the end either way.

questions.question: Complete the function so wait(500) returns a promise that fulfills after 500 ms.
questions.explanation: The executor function receives resolve (and reject) as parameters. Passing resolve to setTimeout fulfills the promise when the timer fires. The parameter name must match the resolve used in the body.

questions.question: This throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'length'). Why?
choices: The first callback doesn't return the fetchOrders promise, so the next then receives undefined
fetchOrders must be called with await
then can only be chained twice
user.id is undefined inside the first callback
questions.explanation: Without return, the chain doesn't wait for fetchOrders and passes undefined along. Write user => fetchOrders(user.id), or add return. await isn't available in a plain callback.

questions.question: What does this log?
questions.explanation: Promise.all keeps results in input order, not completion order. b finished first, but its value still sits in position 1.

questions.question: What does Promise.allSettled produce for a promise that rejected?
questions.explanation: Every entry is an outcome object: { status: "fulfilled", value } or { status: "rejected", reason }. That uniform shape is what lets you handle partial success.

questions.question: Match each combinator to how it settles.

pairs.right: All values in input order, or the first rejection
An outcome object for every promise; never rejects
Like the first promise to settle, either way
The first fulfilled value; rejects only if all reject

questions.explanation: Pick by the question you're asking: need everything (all), want every outcome (allSettled), need the fastest answer or a timeout (race), or need the first success (any).

questions.question: What does this log?
questions.explanation: race settles like whichever promise settles first, and the rejection at 20 ms beats the data at 50 ms. This is exactly how a request timeout is built.

questions.explanation: any ignores rejections as long as something fulfills. The failure at 10 ms is skipped, and c, the first to fulfill at 20 ms, wins.

questions.question: Complete the code so res holds the response, not a pending promise.

questions.question: This logs undefined instead of Ada. What is wrong?
choices: getUser must be declared with an arrow function
getUser returns a promise, so show must be async and use const user = await getUser()
Objects can't be returned from async functions
user.name must be read inside a setTimeout
questions.explanation: user is a Promise, and a Promise has no name property. Awaiting it inside an async show unwraps the value. A timer would only delay the same mistake.

questions.question: About how long does run() take to finish?
questions.explanation: Each await waits for its timer before the next line starts the second one, so the waits add up. await Promise.all([wait(100), wait(100)]) would take about 100 ms. await doesn't block the thread, but it does pause this function.

questions.question: What exactly does await pause, and what keeps running?
questions.answer: await pauses only the async function it's in. The thread is released, so the event loop keeps running other code, timers and events. When the awaited promise settles, the function resumes as a microtask.
questions.explanation: That's why await never freezes a page, and why code after an un-awaited async call runs before that call finishes.

questions.question: fetch("/api/missing") gets a 404 response. What happens to the promise fetch returned?
choices: It rejects with a NotFound error
It fulfills with a Response whose ok is false and status is 404
questions.explanation: fetch only rejects on network failures. HTTP error statuses still produce a Response, so you must check res.ok or res.status and throw yourself.

questions.question: Complete the check so any non-2xx response becomes an error.
questions.explanation: res.ok is true only for statuses 200 to 299, so !res.ok catches every error status, including 500. Checking only for 404 misses server errors, and res itself is always an object.

questions.question: Complete the request so the todo object is sent as JSON.
questions.explanation: The body must be a string, so JSON.stringify turns the object into JSON text. String(todo) would send "[object Object]", and JSON.parse goes the other way, from text to object.

questions.question: Put the steps of fetching JSON safely in order.
items: Call fetch with the URL and await the Response
Check res.ok and throw an error if it's false
Await res.json() to parse the body
questions.explanation: The status check has to happen before you trust the body, and the body needs its own await. Wrap the whole sequence in try/catch to handle both network failures and the errors you throw.

questions.question: This logs [] instead of the three doubled values. Why?
choices: push can't be called inside an async callback
forEach doesn't wait for the async callbacks, so results is logged before any push happens; use for...of with await, or Promise.all with map
results must be declared with let
questions.explanation: Each callback pauses at its await and returns a promise, which forEach ignores. The log runs right away. const results = await Promise.all([1, 2, 3].map(double)) gives [2, 4, 6].

questions.question: This takes about 400 ms, though getProfile and getFeed don't depend on each other and each takes about 200 ms. What is the fix?
questions.code:
const profile = await getProfile(id);
const feed = await getFeed(id);
choices: Start both and wait together: const [profile, feed] = await Promise.all([getProfile(id), getFeed(id)])
questions.explanation: Promise.all lets both requests run at once, so the total is about the slower one, 200 ms. Removing the awaits would leave you holding promises instead of data.

questions.question: In Node.js 15 and later, what happens by default when a promise rejects and nothing ever handles it?
choices: Nothing; the rejection is silently ignored
The process crashes with the error
questions.explanation: Unhandled rejections are fatal in modern Node, and browsers log them as errors. End every chain with a catch, and await async calls inside try/catch.
